To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the use of bioassays for screening phage libraries and for the selection of antibodies is a powerful new tool in the study and purification of uncharacterized proteins that defy conventional techniques.

(1) the combination of bio-assay and phage-display technologies is a powerful strategy to identify and characterise uncharacterised proteins; and (2) the data support suggestions that gonadotrophins surge-attenuation factor (GnSaf) may be structurally similar to serum albumin, or very tightly bound with serum albumin.

we have developed a bioassay-based approach for the identification of antibodies that recognise GnSAF bio-activity, and that we have used these to identify a candidate GnSAF molecule that is structurally related to human serum albumin or tightly bound to serum-albumin.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a novel approach for the identification of bioactive molecules and we believe that this strategy will prove valuable in the study of other bioactive proteins.
the development of new technologies to aid in the isolation and identification of the elusive GnSAF molecule.
the identification of GnSAF, a protein which is believed to be involved in the control of the preovulatory gonadotroph surge and hence ovulation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
GnSAF has been identified as a 66 kDa protein, which is either human serum albumin or a very tightly associated protein.
the GnSAF protein is yet to be isolated and characterised.
we have identified GnSAF as human serum albumin.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

GnSAF is a serum albumin-related protein that is secreted by the granulosa cells in the human ovary and that it acts to suppress the release of gonadotrophic hormones by binding to the GnRH receptors on the gonadotrophs.
GnSAF is a novel, bioactive protein with a molecular weight around 66 kD, and that it may be a serum albumin variant.
GnSAF is not a protein, but a protein complex, possibly with a serum albumin component.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the bioassay is the critical component in this process.

we have shown that bioassay can be used to select antibodies for the isolation of bioactive GnSAf, and we have also demonstrated that GnSAf may be structurally or functionally related to serum albumins.

the use of bioassay to screen for antibodies that can be used for the immunopurification of proteins that are bioactive but not immunogenic is a promising approach to overcome the limitations of conventional approaches.
